content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Draw a box plot from a five-number summary
Read values from a box plot
Compare two datasets using box plots
Identify skewness from a box plot
Link box plots to cumulative frequency graphs
) is a powerful way to display the spread and central tendency of a dataset using just five key values. Box plots are especially useful for comparing distributions side by side.
They are widely used in science, business, and medicine to visualise data spread -- for example, comparing the recovery times of patients on different treatments.

Class B has a higher median (60) than Class A (55), so Class B performed better on average.
Class A: IQR $= 65 - 40 = 25$ Class B: IQR $= 68 - 50 = 18$
Class B has a smaller IQR, so Class B's middle 50% of scores are more consistent.
Class A: Range $= 85 - 20 = 65$ Class B: Range $= 78 - 35 = 43$
Class A has a much larger range, indicating a wider overall spread of scores.
Class B performed better on average (higher median) and was more consistent (smaller IQR and range). Class A had both the lowest and highest individual scores.

Orchard A has a higher median (110 g vs 105 g), so its apples are heavier on average. Orchard A has a larger IQR ($120 - 95 = 25$ vs $115 - 100 = 15$) and range ($140 - 80 = 60$ vs $130 - 90 = 40$), so Orchard B's apples are more consistent in weight.
The length of the box is the IQR ($Q_3 - Q_1$). It represents the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
Draw on a number line from 0 to 60. Left whisker at 5, box from 20 to 38 with median at 28, right whisker at 55.
IQR $= 60 - 40 = 20$. $1.5 \times 20 = 30$. Lower boundary: $40 - 30 = 10$. Upper boundary: $60 + 30 = 90$. Any value below 10 or above 90 is an outlier.

Girls have a higher median (38 vs 35) and higher $Q_1$ (30 vs 28), so girls performed better on average. Boys have a larger IQR ($42 - 28 = 14$ vs $44 - 30 = 14$) -- actually the IQRs are equal. Boys have a larger range ($55 - 15 = 40$ vs $50 - 20 = 30$), indicating more variability overall.
The mean depends on every individual value, but a box plot only shows five summary statistics. Different datasets can have the same box plot but different means.

Yes. A box plot shows five summary statistics, not the sample size. A dataset of 10 values and a dataset of 1000 values could have the same min, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, and max.
